The patients were 61.1 ± 15.1 years old (range,
32-81), and seven were women. Except for one patient with stiff
limb syndrome and one patient with a calpainopathy type of muscle
dystrophy, neurogenic processes were diagnosed in all patients,
namely motor neuron disease (three) or different types of peripheral
nerve disorders (nine). Spontaneous continuous motor unit single
discharges (Videos S1, S2, and S3) were present in various muscles
and were usually identified in only one or two instances per patient.
However, in the patient with HINT1 (histidine triad nucleotide bind-
ing protein 1) polyneuropathy, seven different SCMUSDs were
recorded in two different muscles. The involved MU potentials dis-
charged continuously without silent intervals at a rate of about
6 H Z (6.3 ± 4.0; range, 1.3-18.1). The coefficient of variation was
3.5% ± 1.7%. Stiff limb syndrome (18.1 H Z), amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis (15.5 H Z), or chronic inflammatory demyelinating poly-
neuropathy (11.7 H Z) were diagnosed in patients with relatively
high MU discharge rates. Kennedy syndrome (1.3 H Z), calpainopathy
type of muscle dystrophy (1.7 H Z), or polyneuropathy due to
Sjögren syndrome (3.1 H Z) were diagnosed in patients with espe-
cially low MU discharge rates. There was a significant positive corre-
lation between coefficient of variation and MU discharge frequency
(Figure 1; P < .01; Kendall's τ). Motor unit potential amplitudes were
in the normal range or lower (0.29 ± 0.22 mV). Motor unit potential
duration was usually longer than normal (20.3 ± 12.7 ms). Blocking
within the MUP components was present in eight instances, and
jitter was increased in 12. When an increased jitter was detected,
MUP duration was significantly longer than in those instances with
apparently normal jitter (Figure 2; P < .005, Mann –Whitney U test).
No such difference in MUP duration was noted whether blocking
was present or absent, presumably due to the low number of MUPs
displaying blocking.

4 | DISCUSSION
In contrast to myokymic discharges, which consist of bursts of 2, 3, or
more MUPs from the same MU, SCMUSDs are confined to single MUP
that repeat at relatively constant intervals. Spontaneous continuous
motor unit single discharges have not been observed in patients with
disorders that have finally been diagnosed to be functional in nature.
Therefore, SCMUSD can likely be taken as an abnormal phenomenon.
In our case series, the majority of the diagnoses were neurogenic pro-
cesses. In one patient, a calpainopathy type of muscular dystrophy had
been diagnosed. In calpainopathy, a broad spectrum of symptoms may
be present, and neurogenic phenomena in EMG recordings are not
uncommon.
7 In another patient, stiff limb syndrome was diagnosed.
Other motor hyperexcitability phenomena such as myokymic dis-
charges have been described previously in stiff person syndrome.
1
When the MUPs that were recorded as SCMUSDs were analyzed, the
majority could readily be identified as reinnervation potentials because
of their long durations and the temporal dispersion of the potential
components. The MUPs with a normal duration still could display signs
of impaired neuromuscular transmission such as blocking or an increase
in jitter relative to the potential component that was taken for trigger-
ing. Only excessively increased jitter could be identified reliably. Such
jitter was more often present in MUPs with a pathologically long dura-
tion than in MUPs with a normal duration (Figure 2). Thus, both an
increase in jitter and the presence of MUPs with an increased duration
can be taken as further hints that axonal sprouting may play a crucial
role in SCMUSD generation, at least in peripheral neurogenic processes.
The expression of ion channels has been shown to be altered in growth
cones of sprouting peripheral nerve axons.
8 Such alterations in ion
channel expression may be important in generating motor axonal spon-
taneous activity. The SCMUSD frequency of about 6 H Z presumably
corresponds to the specific depolarization characteristics of the
involved ion channels. In contrast to pathological muscle fiber sponta-
neous activity such as positive sharp waves or fibrillation potentials that
are characterized by constancy in repetition rate, SCMUSD repetition is
characterized by a somewhat less constant discharge rate with a coeffi-
cient of variation of 3.5% ± 1.7%. Whether this slight inconstancy in
SCMUSD generation is due to differences in depolarizing membrane
currents through membrane ion channels, inconstancies of action
potential propagation, differences in the amounts of transmitter quanta
released into the synaptic cleft remains to be established. A discharge
rate of 5.2 ± 1.6 H Z (coefficient of variation 5.4% ± 1.6%), which is
close to that reported here, has been detected in leg muscles after
long-lasting spinal cord injury. Thus, the similarity of the SCMUSD find-
ings in neurogenic processes and in the patient with stiff limb syndrome
may be due to similarities between axonal sprouts and in ventral horn
cells deafferented from upper motor neuron input. The coefficient of
variation observed in our investigation is definitively smaller than what
has been shown for voluntarily recruited MUs, which are in the range
of 9% to 47%.
9 This difference in coefficient of variation may facilitate
the distinction from voluntarily recruited MUs that might contaminate
recordings from incompletely relaxed patients.

In conclusion, SCMUSDs add to the spectrum of MUH phenom-
ena with continuous MU activity. Spontaneous continuous motor unit
single discharges appear to occur in a spectrum of diseases similar to
those associated with myokymic discharges.
